name: Sep
baseline: CsvHelper (the most widely used .NET CSV parsing library)
workload: Parsing CSV rows into columns/floats (PackageAssets and Floats benchmarks, 50000 rows, with/without trimming and unescaping) using BenchmarkDotNet on .NET 9.0
claimed_speedup: ~9-11x faster than CsvHelper for PackageAssets-with-quotes parsing (e.g. 12.92ms vs 142.26ms on AMD EPYC 7763); README also states 'up to 35x faster than CsvHelper' for the Floats benchmark with ParallelEnumerate
compiler_and_flags: .NET 9.0.X runtime, BenchmarkDotNet, GC DATAS mode disabled (GarbageCollectionAdaptationMode=0)
hardware: Multiple platforms tested: AMD EPYC 7763 (Ubuntu 22.04, virtual), AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 7840U, AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, Apple M1 (virtual), plus a 'Cobalt.100' ARM platform
tradeoffs: Opinionated API tailored to ML use cases, no automatic quote unescaping/trimming by default (must opt in), default separator is ';' not ',', requires modern C#/.NET (Span<T>, generic math)
caveats: Benchmark author is the library's own maintainer (first-party); comparison also includes Sylvan (a fast third CSV library) alongside CsvHelper, and CsvHelper is not tuned for these specific low-level access patterns; different feature sets (e.g. CsvHelper supports more backwards compatibility) mean the comparison isn't perfectly apples-to-apples per the README's own disclaimer

name: go-simdcsv
workload: ReadAll throughput on synthetic CSV files with varying quote density (unquoted, 10%/40% quoted, all-quoted) at 10K and 100K rows, using AVX-512 SIMD scanning vs Go's encoding/csv
claimed_speedup: +35% faster (unquoted, 10K and 100K rows), +8% faster (10% quoted, 100K rows), +6% faster (40% quoted, 100K rows); notably -30% slower on all-quoted-fields data
tradeoffs: Explicitly marked experimental, requires bleeding-edge Go 1.26 with an experimental SIMD flag, AMD64-only (falls back to scalar without AVX-512, so no speedup on Apple Silicon or older CPUs), 'not recommended for production use', and is slower than stdlib on heavily-quoted data
caveats: Modest speedup (6-35%) rather than dramatic; the project's own README frankly reports a regression case (-30%) for all-quoted fields, which is honest but limits the generality of the 'faster' claim; very new/small project
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "csv parser" simd --sort stars

name: zsv (zsv+lib)
baseline: DuckDB CSV reader and Python Polars read_csv (also benchmarked against BurntSushi/xsv, qsv, and xan)
workload: count (row counting) and select (full parse + CSV re-output) on a 433MB/~9.5M-row worldcitiespop.csv-derived file and separate 118-127MB unquoted/sparsely-quoted/standard-quoted/nonstandard-quoted datasets (500000 rows x 20 cols), single- and multi-threaded
claimed_speedup: zsv --parallel fastest for count (e.g. 0.008s vs DuckDB 0.049s, Polars 0.092s on unquoted data, ~14.3 GB/s throughput); memory footprint 52x smaller than DuckDB and 324x smaller than Polars in single-threaded mode
hardware: Apple M3 Pro (single-threaded runs), cross-checked on Linux/Intel
tradeoffs: The fast/SIMD parser mode produces incorrect output on nonstandard-quoted (non-RFC-4180) CSV, so full correctness requires falling back to the slower 'compat' parser; DuckDB and Polars were given 'handicaps' (relaxed quote/newline handling) in this comparison to make them competitive at all
caveats: First-party benchmark (zsv's own repo); build compiler and optimization flags for the zsv binary itself are not stated in the results doc (only CPU and tool versions), so this is capped below Tier A/B per methodology rules; DuckDB and Polars are dataframe engines with much broader scope than zsv, so the comparison favors a narrowly-scoped CSV tool
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos csv --topic csv --sort stars

name: xan
baseline: BurntSushi/xsv and Python Polars/DuckDB CSV readers (independent comparison; xan itself targets csvkit-style CSV toolkits)
workload: Same zsv-authored count/select benchmark: 'select' operation on unquoted and sparsely-quoted ~118MB CSV data (500000 rows x 20 cols)
claimed_speedup: xan is the fastest tool for 'select' on unquoted (0.077s) and sparsely-quoted (0.081s) datasets in this independent shootout, beating zsv-fast (0.097s/0.105s single-threaded), xsv, polars and duckdb on those specific datasets; xan fails (produces incorrect output) on nonstandard-quoted data
tradeoffs: xan's win is workload-specific (only on unquoted/sparsely-quoted data for 'select'); it produces incorrect output on nonstandard-quoted CSV, same limitation zsv-fast has; xan's own README/docs do not present this benchmark themselves
caveats: This is evidence harvested from a shootout run by a different, independent project (liquidaty/zsv), not xan's own claim -- tier B because it's an independent comparison with public code, versions and CPU stated, but the compiler/build flags used for the xan binary are not stated
found_via: GitHub: liquidaty/zsv benchmark results (harvested shootout winner) after gh search repos csv --topic csv --sort stars

name: simd-csv (Rust crate)
baseline: csv crate (docs.rs/csv, i.e. BurntSushi/rust-csv, the de facto standard Rust CSV library)
workload: Streaming CSV parsing from SSD across 10 real/synthetic files (200MB-11GB, e.g. articles.csv 11GB/3M rows, tweets.csv 6.5GB/~7M rows, worldcitiespop.csv 500MB) comparing split/zero_copy/copy reader variants to the csv crate's Reader, on x86_64 with AVX2
claimed_speedup: Up to ~6.0x faster (tweets.csv, split mode), ~4.7-4.8x (articles.csv), ~2.0-3.1x on most other files, dropping to ~1.0-1.2x (near parity) on quote-always.csv and worst-case.csv
compiler_and_flags: Rust, x86_64 with AVX2 (RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' explicitly stated as not required)
tradeoffs: Author's own README says explicitly not to expect the 16-32x gains of a true SIMD parser like simdjson; performance is very data-dependent (near-1x on worst-case/quote-always files); less flexible/user-friendly API than the csv crate; built specifically to serve the xan CLI tool's needs
caveats: First-party benchmark with no specific CPU model stated (only 'x86_64 with avx2 support'), so it is capped at Tier C; numbers are approximate ('~4.8x') rather than exact figures
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "csv reader" rust --sort stars

name: zsv-ruby
workload: Parsing CSV files of 1K, 10K and 100K rows (5-10 cols) via Ruby native-extension bindings to the zsv C library, measured in iterations/second, vs Ruby's stdlib CSV class
claimed_speedup: 6.20x faster (1K rows), 5.27x faster (10K rows), 5.00x faster (100K rows), 4.33x faster (10K rows with headers); also ~82.6% less memory and ~57% fewer string allocations
tradeoffs: Thin Ruby wrapper around the C zsv library (see liquidaty/zsv entry in this same batch); inherits zsv's SIMD-dependent performance characteristics; very new and low-adoption gem, README states it was built with Claude Code
caveats: No CPU model or compiler flags stated for the benchmark, so it cannot exceed Tier C; extremely small/new project (17 stars, single author) so treat numbers as unverified by outside parties; the underlying speedup is really zsv's, wrapped for Ruby
